questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Constant-time 128-bit comparison is core in cryptography and DB internals to avoid timing channels; probe understanding of lexicographic, boundary handling without branches.

## Key Concepts
- Branchless logic with masks
- Lexicographic 128-bit comparison
- Handling hi/lo boundaries in constant time

## Code Example
```javascript
typedef struct { uint64_t hi; uint64_t lo; } uint128;
static inline int8_t cmp128(uint128 a, uint128 b) {
  int hi = (a.hi > b.hi) - (a.hi < b.hi); // -1,0,1
  int lo = (a.lo > b.lo) - (a.lo < b.lo);
  int m = -(int)(hi != 0); // -1 when hi != 0, else 0
  return (int8_t)((hi & m) | (lo & ~m));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt this to return a sign-agnostic 0/1/2 encoding for a hash comparison?
- Could you prove this runs in constant time regardless of inputs and compiler optimizations?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This tests precise bit manipulation skills for rearranging 8-byte blocks without loops, essential for portable endianness handling in systems programming.

## Key Concepts

- Byte-level masking with 64-bit constants
- Multi-stage shuffles to minimize operations
- Endianness portability across platforms

## Code Example

```c
uint64_t bswap64(uint64_t x) {
  x = ((x & 0x00FF00FF00FF00FFULL) << 8) | ((x >> 8) & 0x00FF00FF00FF00FFULL);
  x = ((x & 0x0000FFFF0000FFFFULL) << 16) | ((x >> 16) & 0x0000FFFF0000FFFFULL);
  return (x << 32) | (x >> 32);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you verify correctness of this implementation?
- What are the trade-offs between this approach and using built-in byte swap functions?
- How would this differ on a little-endian vs big-endian system?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Assesses ability to manipulate a 128-bit value using two 64-bit parts and leverage available intrinsics for performance. It tests understanding of bit significance ordering and boundary cases (zero input).

## Key Concepts

- 128-bit represented as two 64-bit words (lo then hi) and how trailing zeros map across the boundary
- Using 64-bit ctz intrinsics to build a 128-bit result in constant time
- Correct handling of the all-zero input returning 128

## Code Example

```c
int trailingZeroCount128(uint128 x) {
  if (x.lo != 0) return __builtin_ctzll(x.lo);
  if (x.hi != 0) return 64 + __builtin_ctzll(x.hi);
  return 128;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you implement this without compiler intrinsics?
- How would you port the approach to a 256-bit representation?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to decompose a 128-bit value into fixed lanes and reconstruct a rotated layout using only bitwise ops and masking, without branches.

## Key Concepts
- Lane extraction with masks, 32-bit blocks
- Fixed-layout reconstruction; endianness awareness
- Constant-time block-wise permutation

## Code Example
```javascript
uint128 rotateBlocks128(uint128 x) { uint64_t A = x.lo & 0xFFFFFFFFULL; uint64_t B = (x.lo >> 32) & 0xFFFFFFFFULL; uint64_t C = x.hi & 0xFFFFFFFFULL; uint64_t D = (x.hi >> 32) & 0xFFFFFFFFULL; uint128 r; r.lo = (A << 32) | D; r.hi = (C << 32) | B; return r; }
```

## Follow-up Questions
